name: Zebu cattle domestication in the Indus Valley
summary: Humped zebu cattle were domesticated in the Indus Valley about 8000 years ago and later became the cattle of South Asia and much of the tropics.
description: A 2023 genome study, citing archaeological work, places domesticated indicine (zebu) cattle in the Indus Valley of modern Pakistan about 8000 years before present, earlier than in South India or the middle Ganges, and calls the valley their domestication centre. It reports that they began to spread from the valley about 5000 years before present and reached south-west, central and east Asia and Africa.

impact.note: The source reports zebu spreading from the Indus Valley across South Asia and into south-west, central and east Asia and Africa, so many societies on two continents; a large herd animal was a new capability for these farmers, and the heat-tolerant breeds and crosses are its direct successors.

date.label: about 8000 years before present (c. 6050 BCE)
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

events.statement: A genome study, citing archaeological evidence, places domesticated indicine cattle in the Indus Valley at about 8000 years before present (c. 6050 BCE, counting from 1950).

evidence.supports: Archaeological evidence indicates the presence of domesticated indicine cattle earlier in the Indus Valley (~8000 YBP) than in South India (~5000 YBP) and the middle Ganges (~4000 YBP)

date.label: about 5000 years before present (c. 3050 BCE)
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

events.statement: Indicine cattle began to spread from the Indus Valley about 5000 years before present (c. 3050 BCE, counting from 1950), later reaching south-west and central Asia, east Asia and Africa.

evidence.supports: The global dispersal of indicine cattle started in the Indus Valley at ~5000 YBP, followed by their spread into Southwest and Central Asia, East Asia, and Africa between 4000 and 1300 YBP

earliest_record.rationale: The earliest dated evidence found for this capability in this community. No review has yet confirmed that nothing earlier exists.

unresolved.note: The date and place rest on a genome paper's summary of archaeological work; Mehrgarh and Meadow's bone-size evidence were not opened and should replace this as the primary evidence.
The Indus Valley coordinates are a rough regional centre, not a site.
Whether the first zebu herders already knew of taurine cattle or of herded goats and sheep from the west is not settled here; Chen et al. 2010 on zebu mitochondrial DNA was not opened.

research.note: The source treats the Indus Valley as the domestication centre of indicine cattle, about 2000 years after taurine cattle, but does not say whether its herders knew of cattle keeping further west.
